## Impact Evaluation

**Source:** `js/target.js` → `evaluateImpact(speed, mass, material, impactMultiplier)`
**Priority:** High

### Expected behaviours

| # | Behaviour | Test type | Priority |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Returns SHATTER when impulse (speed × mass × multiplier) ≥ material.strength | Happy path | High |
| 2 | Returns CRACK when impulse ≥ crackThreshold but < strength | Happy path | High |
| 3 | Returns SURVIVE when impulse < crackThreshold | Happy path | High |
| 4 | Returns SHATTER at exact strength boundary | Boundary | High |
| 5 | Returns CRACK at exact crackThreshold boundary | Boundary | High |
| 6 | Returns SURVIVE at one below crackThreshold | Boundary | High |
| 7 | Returns SURVIVE when speed = 0 | Unhappy path | High |
| 8 | Returns SURVIVE when mass = 0 | Unhappy path | High |
| 9 | Returns SURVIVE when impactMultiplier = 0 | Unhappy path | High |
| 10 | impactMultiplier scales outcome (heavy yoyo shatters what standard cracks) | Cross-variant | High |

### Edge cases and unhappy paths

- Zero speed, zero mass, zero multiplier — all should SURVIVE (impulse = 0)
- Very large speed — should SHATTER any material
- `impactMultiplier` of 2.2 (heavy yoyo) should push borderline hits into SHATTER

---

## Fragment Vertices

**Source:** `js/target.js` → `getFragmentVerts(count)`
**Priority:** Medium

### Expected behaviours

| # | Behaviour | Test type | Priority |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Returns 10-polygon set when count ≥ 10 | Happy path | Medium |
| 2 | Returns 6-polygon set when count < 10 | Happy path | Medium |
| 3 | Returns 6-polygon set at count = 6 (exact match) | Boundary | Medium |
| 4 | Returns 6-polygon set at count = 9 (just below 10) | Boundary | Medium |
| 5 | Returns 6-polygon set at count = 0 (steel has 0 fragments) | Unhappy path | Medium |
| 6 | Each polygon is an array of [x, y] vertex pairs | Structure | Medium |

### Edge cases and unhappy paths

- count = 0 (steel material) — must not crash; returns 6-frag set
- count = 11 — returns 10-frag set (threshold is ≥ 10, not exact)

---

## Crack Pattern Generation

**Source:** `js/target.js` → `generateCrackPattern(count)`
**Priority:** Medium

### Expected behaviours

| # | Behaviour | Test type | Priority |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Returns array of exactly `count` lines | Happy path | High |
| 2 | Each line has `angle` (number) and `len` (number) | Structure | High |
| 3 | `len` is within [0.2, 0.55] for all lines | Boundary | High |
| 4 | `angle` is within [0, 2π] for all lines | Boundary | Medium |
| 5 | count = 0 returns empty array | Unhappy path | High |
| 6 | Default call `generateCrackPattern(6)` returns 6 lines | Happy path | Medium |

### Setup requirements

- Use `vi.spyOn(Math, 'random')` to control randomness for deterministic boundary checks

---

## Level Lookup

**Source:** `js/levels.js` → `getLevel(id)`
**Priority:** High

### Expected behaviours

| # | Behaviour | Test type | Priority |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Returns level object for valid id = 1 | Happy path | High |
| 2 | Returns level object for valid id = 2 | Happy path | High |
| 3 | Returns LEVELS[0] (fallback) for unknown id = 99 | Unhappy path | High |
| 4 | Returns LEVELS[0] (fallback) for id = 0 | Boundary | High |
| 5 | Returned level has required fields: id, name, pivot, targets, parScore, stringLength | Structure | High |
| 6 | pivot has x and y fields (both numbers in 0–1 range) | Structure | Medium |
| 7 | Each target has shape, x, y, material fields | Structure | Medium |

### Edge cases and unhappy paths

- id = 0 — not a real level, falls through to fallback
- id = 999 — unknown id, falls through to fallback
- Negative id — falls through to fallback

---

## Progress Save / Load

**Source:** `js/levels.js` → `saveProgress(levelId, score)`, `loadProgress()`
**Priority:** High

### Expected behaviours

| # | Behaviour | Test type | Priority |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `loadProgress` returns `{}` when localStorage is empty | Happy path | High |
| 2 | `saveProgress` stores a high score for a level | Happy path | High |
| 3 | `loadProgress` retrieves a previously saved score | Happy path | High |
| 4 | `saveProgress` overwrites when new score > existing | Happy path | High |
| 5 | `saveProgress` does NOT overwrite when new score ≤ existing | Unhappy path | High |
| 6 | `saveProgress` advances `unlockedLevel` to levelId + 1 | Happy path | High |
| 7 | `saveProgress` does not reduce `unlockedLevel` below current | Unhappy path | High |
| 8 | `loadProgress` returns `{}` on corrupt (non-JSON) localStorage | Unhappy path | High |

### Setup requirements

- Clear `localStorage` in `beforeEach` to isolate tests
- To simulate corrupt data: `localStorage.setItem('yoyo_progress', 'NOT_JSON')`

---

## Input — Angular Speed & State

**Source:** `js/input.js` → `init()`, `getAngularSpeed()`, `isMouseDown()`, `getCurrentAngle()`
**Priority:** High

### Expected behaviours

| # | Behaviour | Test type | Priority |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `getAngularSpeed()` returns 0 immediately after `init()` | Happy path | High |
| 2 | `isMouseDown()` returns false immediately after `init()` | Happy path | High |
| 3 | `getCurrentAngle()` returns π/2 immediately after `init()` (start below pivot) | Happy path | High |
| 4 | After mousedown on canvas, `isMouseDown()` returns true | Happy path | High |
| 5 | After mousedown then mouseup, `isMouseDown()` returns false | Happy path | High |
| 6 | Release callback is called with `vx`, `vy`, `speed`, `angle` fields | Happy path | High |
| 7 | Release speed is clamped to variant `maxSpeed` | Boundary | High |
| 8 | `getAngularSpeed()` returns value in [0, 1] range | Boundary | High |

# Commit Skill

## Purpose

To produce clean, readable, well-scoped git commits that are easy to parse
in code review and git history. Every commit request must follow this workflow
in full — no steps may be skipped unless explicitly instructed by the user.

---

## Step 1 — Survey the working tree

Run these commands in parallel:

```bash
git status
git diff
git diff --cached
```

Read the full diff carefully. Understand **what changed and why** before
proceeding. Do not write a commit message until the diff has been reviewed.

---

## Step 2 — Check for pre-commit blockers

Scan the staged and unstaged changes for the following. If any are found,
flag them to the user and resolve before committing:

| Check | What to look for |
|---|---|
| Debug code | `console.log`, `debugger`, `TODO`, `FIXME`, `HACK` left in production paths |
| Secrets / env files | `.env`, `.env.local`, `*.key`, `*.pem`, `credentials*`, `secrets*` staged or touched |
| Build check | Run the project's build command to confirm it still compiles cleanly |
| Accidental bulk adds | Ensure `node_modules/`, `*.db`, `*.db-wal`, `*.db-shm` are not staged |

If a blocker is found, stop and report it. Do not proceed until the user
confirms the issue is resolved or intentionally accepted.

---

## Step 3 — Segregate changes into logical commits

Examine the diff for changes that serve **different purposes**. Split into
separate commits when changes fall into clearly different categories. Use
judgment — do not split what belongs together.

**Split when changes are:**
- Different in type and unrelated in purpose (e.g. a bug fix + a new feature)
- Touching different subsystems for different reasons
- Mix of functional change and documentation/config update with no coupling

**Keep together when:**
- A feature spans multiple files but is one cohesive unit of work
- A fix requires touching both the implementation and its test/config
- Changes are tightly coupled and would be meaningless or broken in isolation

For each logical group, stage only those files, then proceed through
Steps 4–5 before moving to the next group.

---

## Step 4 — Build the commit message interactively

Each of the 6 substeps below requires a suggestion followed by explicit user
approval before proceeding. Present the suggestion clearly, then **pause and
wait**. Do not advance to the next substep until the user confirms or amends.

---

### 4.1 — Review staged changes

Run `git diff --staged` and display the output. Write a brief plain-English
summary of what files changed and what the changes do. Ask the user to confirm
this summary is accurate before continuing.

> "Here's what's staged: [summary]. Does this look right before we build
> the commit message?"

**Wait for approval.**

---

### 4.2 — Identify commit type

Based on the staged diff, propose a Conventional Commits type with a one-line
rationale. Ask the user to confirm or change it.

| Type | Use for |
|---|---|
| `feat` | New feature or capability |
| `fix` | Bug fix |
| `refactor` | Code change that neither fixes a bug nor adds a feature |
| `chore` | Tooling, dependencies, config, build changes |
| `docs` | Documentation only |
| `style` | Formatting, whitespace — no logic change |
| `perf` | Performance improvement |
| `test` | Adding or correcting tests |

> "Suggested type: `fix` — this corrects incorrect behaviour in the parser.
> Agree, or would you like a different type?"

**Wait for approval.**

---

### 4.3 — Determine scope

Propose a scope based on the primary subsystem or module touched. Scope is
optional but strongly encouraged. Use short, lowercase identifiers that match
the project's own naming conventions (e.g. `api`, `ui`, `db`, `auth`).

Ask the user to confirm or change it.

> "Suggested scope: `api` — the changes are isolated to the API layer.
> Agree, or would you like a different scope (or none)?"

**Wait for approval.**

---

### 4.4 — Write the subject line

Propose a subject line following these rules:
- Max **50 characters** (hard limit — count carefully)
- Imperative mood: "add", "fix", "remove" — not "added", "fixes", "removes"
- No trailing period
- Lowercase after the colon

Show the full first line as it will appear, with a character count:

> "Suggested subject (43 chars):
> `fix(api): handle missing field in response`
> Approve, or suggest a revision?"

**Wait for approval.**

---

### 4.5 — Write the commit body

Draft a body paragraph explaining **why** the change was made and what impact
it has. Do not just restate the subject line. Rules:
- One blank line between subject and body
- Wrap at ~72 characters per line
- Explain the problem being solved, not just the solution
- Keep it human-readable for future reviewers

Present the full draft body and ask for approval or amendments:

> "Suggested body:
> [draft body text]
> Approve, or would you like any changes?"

**Wait for approval.**

---

### 4.6 — Note breaking changes

Assess whether the changes break any existing API contracts, data schemas,
or public interfaces.

If a breaking change exists, propose a `BREAKING CHANGE:` footer:

```
BREAKING CHANGE: <what broke and what callers must do differently>
```

If no breaking change exists, state that clearly and confirm with the user.

> "No breaking changes detected — existing consumers are unaffected.
> Confirm, or is there a breaking change to note?"

**Wait for approval.**

---

### Assembled message

Once all 6 substeps are approved, display the complete commit message in full
for a final review before any git command is run:

```
<type>(<scope>): <subject>

<body>

[BREAKING CHANGE: <note>  ← only if applicable]
```

> "Here is the full commit message. Ready to commit?"

**Wait for final approval before proceeding to Step 5.**

---

## Step 5 — Create the commit

Use a heredoc to preserve formatting exactly:

```bash
git commit -m "$(cat <<'EOF'
<type>(<scope>): <subject>

<body>
EOF
)"
```

After the commit, run `git status` to confirm success and a clean tree
(or remaining unstaged changes for subsequent commits).

---

## Step 6 — Handle multiple logical groups

If Step 3 identified multiple logical groups, repeat Steps 4–5 for each
remaining group in order from most foundational to most surface-level
(e.g. backend before frontend, core logic before docs).

---

## Constraints

- Never use `git add -A` or `git add .` without reviewing what will be staged
- Never use `--no-verify` or `--amend` on published commits unless explicitly requested
- Never push to remote unless the user explicitly asks
- Never commit `.env`, `.env.local`, `*.db`, `*.db-wal`, `*.db-shm`, or `node_modules/`

# /impl-review

Post-implementation review — checks divergence from the brainstorm plan, updates
documentation on the spot, and signals the commit can proceed. Run before every commit.

## Usage
```
/impl-review        # run after completing an implementation task
```

---

## Step 1 — Read context

Read the following before doing anything else:
- `project-state.json` — most recent brainstorm decisions entry, action plan item statuses (if present)
- `git diff HEAD` — what actually changed in this implementation (if a git repo)
- `CLAUDE.md` and `ARCHITECTURE.md` (if present) — current documented state

If no brainstorm decisions entry exists, note this and proceed with the checklist only.

---

## Step 2 — AI divergence assessment

Compare the git diff to the most recent brainstorm decisions entry. Present a
plain-English summary:

> "Based on the changes, here's what was built: [X].
> The planned approach was: [Y].
> Potential divergences: [Z — or 'None detected']."

Present this summary before proceeding to the checklist.

---

## Step 3 — Fixed checklist

Run these three questions one at a time:

1. **Plan accuracy** — "Does the summary above accurately reflect what was built, or did
   something diverge from the plan?"
2. **Dependencies** — "Were any new dependencies added beyond what was planned?"
3. **Contracts** — "Did any API contracts, schemas, or component boundaries change beyond
   what was planned?"

Record any confirmed divergences or additions for Step 4.

---

## Step 4 — Doc updates

For each confirmed finding from Steps 2–3, propose one change at a time and wait for
confirmation before applying:

**decisions log** (`project-state.json`) — if a pivot was made, append an entry:
```json
{
  "date": "<YYYY-MM-DD>",
  "decision": "<what changed from the original plan>",
  "rationale": "<why the pivot was made>"
}
```

**action plan** (`project-state.json`) — mark completed items as `"status": "completed"`.

**`CLAUDE.md`** — if the tech stack, key files, or guidelines changed, update only the
affected section. Do not rewrite the whole file.

**`ARCHITECTURE.md`** — if components, data flows, integrations, or API endpoints changed,
update only the affected sections. Do not rewrite the whole file.

If no changes are needed, state this clearly:
> "No documentation updates required — implementation matches the plan."

---

## Step 5 — Signal completion

Create the review flag so the pre-commit hook knows this step was completed:
```bash
touch /tmp/claude-post-impl-review.flag
```

Report a one-line summary:
> "Implementation review complete. [N doc update(s) applied / No updates needed.]
> Ready to commit — run /commit."

# /brainstorm

Mandatory design gate for new features, components, and non-trivial implementation tasks.
Explores intent, surfaces approaches, and gets design approval before any implementation begins.

## Usage
```
/brainstorm [topic]     # start a brainstorm session for a specific topic
/brainstorm             # start with the current action plan item
```

---

## Hard Gate

Do NOT write code, scaffold files, or take any implementation action until a design has been
presented and the user has given explicit approval. This applies to every project and every
task regardless of apparent simplicity.

---

## Step 1 — Scope check

Assess whether the task warrants a brainstorm session.

**Always brainstorm (never skip unilaterally):**
- New features or user-facing capabilities
- New components, services, or modules
- API or schema changes
- Integrations with external systems
- Refactors that affect how multiple parts of the system interact

**Potentially skippable — ask the user first:**
- Single-file edits with no API, interface, or schema changes
- Bug fixes where the root cause and fix are both unambiguous
- Config or documentation-only changes
- Tasks the user has already described in sufficient implementation detail

If the task falls in the potentially skippable category:
> "This looks like it might be straightforward enough to skip brainstorming — [one-sentence
> reason]. Worth going through the design process, or shall we proceed directly?"

Wait for the user's response. Only skip with explicit confirmation. If in doubt, brainstorm.

---

## Step 2 — Explore context

Read the following before asking any questions:
- `CLAUDE.md` — project overview, constraints, tech stack, guidelines
- `project-state.json` — current activity, action plan, decisions log, open questions (if present)
- Recent commits: `git log --oneline -10` — what has changed recently (if a git repo)

Use this context to avoid asking questions the codebase already answers.

---

## Step 3 — Clarifying questions

Ask one question at a time. Stop when you understand:
- **Purpose** — what problem does this solve, and for whom?
- **Constraints** — technical, time, or scope limits
- **Success criteria** — how will you know it's done?

Target 2–4 questions. Do not ask about things already clear from context.

---

## Step 4 — Propose approaches

Present 2–3 distinct approaches with trade-offs. Lead with a recommendation:

> "I'd recommend **[approach]** — [one-line reason]. Here are the options:
>
> **A — [Name]:** [description]. Trade-off: [pro vs. con].
> **B — [Name]:** [description]. Trade-off: [pro vs. con].
> **C — [Name]:** [description]. Trade-off: [pro vs. con]."

Wait for the user to select or redirect before continuing.

---

## Step 5 — Present design

Present the design in sections, confirming each before moving on. Scale each section to its
complexity — a few sentences for simple changes, more detail for complex ones.

Cover in order:
1. **What's being built** — the feature or component in plain terms
2. **How it fits the existing architecture** — where it lives, what it touches, what it doesn't
3. **Implementation steps** — the first 3–5 concrete tasks

Ask after each section:
> "Does this section look right before I continue?"

---

## Step 6 — Hard gate

Once all sections are presented, request explicit approval:
> "That's the full design. Approve to proceed, or let me know what to revisit."

Do not begin implementation until the user explicitly approves.

---

## Step 7 — Update project state

If a `project-state.json` exists in the project root, after approval:

1. Append a `decisions` log entry:
   ```json
   {
     "date": "<YYYY-MM-DD>",
   ```

From the codebase: the yoyo is drawn entirely with Canvas 2D procedural shapes in `renderer.js` — no sprite assets. The physics body is a circle. Two variants exist (standard / iron) differentiated by mass and size. The "yoyo" concept is woven into variable names, UI copy, level hints, the game title, and `CLAUDE.md`.

**Step 3 — Clarifying questions**

**Question 1 of 2:** How should the rat be drawn?

- **Procedural Canvas 2D** — draw a rat shape using arcs, lines, and fills (body, ears, tail, eyes). No external assets needed, fits the current approach.
- **Emoji rendered to canvas** — draw the 🐀 emoji via `ctx.fillText`. Trivial to implement but rendering quality varies by OS/browser and the size is fixed.
- **Image/sprite** — load a PNG. Adds an asset pipeline concern to a currently asset-free project.

**Question 2 of 2:** How broad is the retheme? The yoyo concept appears in the game title ("Yoyo Smash"), UI copy, level hints, variable names, and `CLAUDE.md`. What's in scope?

- **Visual only** — redraw the swung object as a rat, rename the variants to match (e.g. "small rat" / "big rat"). Everything else stays as-is.
- **Full surface retheme** — new game title, UI copy, level hint text, and variant names all updated to match the rat theme. Internal variable names (`yoyoHp`, `yoyoBody`) left as-is since they're internal.
- **Full retheme + internal rename** — as above, plus rename internal variables and functions to rat-centric names (`ratHp`, `ratBody`, `spawnRat`, etc.).

**Step 4 — Proposed approaches**

I'd recommend **B — Layered** — separates player-visible changes from internal renames, making each commit independently reviewable and testable. Here are the options:

**A — Single pass:** Rename everything — variables, functions, UI copy, file exports, CSS classes, CLAUDE.md — in one branch. Complete and consistent, but a large diff that's hard to review and any mid-pass error affects everything.

**B — Layered (recommended):** Two commits on one branch. Commit 1: UI copy, game title, picker labels, level hints, variant names, and the rat drawing in `renderer.js`. Commit 2: internal renames (`yoyoBody → ratBody`, `yoyoHp → ratHp`, `spawnYoyo → spawnRat`, CSS classes, file exports, `CLAUDE.md`). Each commit leaves the game in a working state; the visual change can be browser-tested before touching internals.

content.text:
# /brainstorm

Mandatory design gate for new features, components, and non-trivial implementation tasks.
Explores intent, surfaces approaches, and gets design approval before any implementation begins.

## Usage
```
/brainstorm [topic]     # start a brainstorm session for a specific topic
/brainstorm             # start with the current action plan item
```

---

## Hard Gate

Do NOT write code, scaffold files, or take any implementation action until a design has been
presented and the user has given explicit approval. This applies to every project and every
task regardless of apparent simplicity.

---

## Step 1 — Scope check

Assess whether the task warrants a brainstorm session.

**Always brainstorm (never skip unilaterally):**
- New features or user-facing capabilities
- New components, services, or modules
- API or schema changes
- Integrations with external systems
- Refactors that affect how multiple parts of the system interact

**Potentially skippable — ask the user first:**
- Single-file edits with no API, interface, or schema changes
- Bug fixes where the root cause and fix are both unambiguous
- Config or documentation-only changes
- Tasks the user has already described in sufficient implementation detail

If the task falls in the potentially skippable category:
> "This looks like it might be straightforward enough to skip brainstorming — [one-sentence
> reason]. Worth going through the design process, or shall we proceed directly?"

Wait for the user's response. Only skip with explicit confirmation. If in doubt, brainstorm.

---

## Step 2 — Explore context

Read the following before asking any questions:
- `CLAUDE.md` — project overview, constraints, tech stack, guidelines
- `project-state.json` — current activity, action plan, decisions log, open questions (if present)
- Recent commits: `git log --oneline -10` — what has changed recently (if a git repo)

Use this context to avoid asking questions the codebase already answers.

---

## Step 3 — Clarifying questions

Ask one question at a time. Stop when you understand:
- **Purpose** — what problem does this solve, and for whom?
- **Constraints** — technical, time, or scope limits
- **Success criteria** — how will you know it's done?

Target 2–4 questions. Do not ask about things already clear from context.

---

## Step 4 — Propose approaches

Present 2–3 distinct approaches with trade-offs. Lead with a recommendation:

> "I'd recommend **[approach]** — [one-line reason]. Here are the options:
>
> **A — [Name]:** [description]. Trade-off: [pro vs. con].
> **B — [Name]:** [description]. Trade-off: [pro vs. con].
> **C — [Name]:** [description]. Trade-off: [pro vs. con]."

Wait for the user to select or redirect before continuing.

---

## Step 5 — Present design

Present the design in sections, confirming each before moving on. Scale each section to its
complexity — a few sentences for simple changes, more detail for complex ones.

Cover in order:
1. **What's being built** — the feature or component in plain terms
2. **How it fits the existing architecture** — where it lives, what it touches, what it doesn't
3. **Implementation steps** — the first 3–5 concrete tasks

Ask after each section:
> "Does this section look right before I continue?"

---

## Step 6 — Hard gate

Once all sections are presented, request explicit approval:
> "That's the full design. Approve to proceed, or let me know what to revisit."

Do not begin implementation until the user explicitly approves.

---

## Step 7 — Update project state

If a `project-state.json` exists in the project root, after approval:

1. Append a `decisions` log entry:
   ```json
   {
     "date": "<YYYY-MM-DD>",
     "decision": "<one-line description of the chosen approach>",
     "rationale": "<why this approach was chosen over the alternatives>"
   }
   ```

2. Add concrete implementation steps from the approved design as new `pending` entries in
   the action plan. Assign sequential IDs continuing from the current highest. Mark any
   item the design supersedes as `"status": "superseded"` rather than removing it.
   Set the first new task as `current_activity`.

3. Report:
   > "Design approved and logged. Action plan updated with [N] implementation tasks.
   > Ready to build."


ARGUMENTS: Rethink level design and progression system for Rat Smash

**Step 2 — Context**

Current levels: 5 linear stages (Greenhouse → Scrapyard → Crystal Palace → Foundry → Wrecking Yard), each a static arrangement of glass/wood/steel rectangles. Progression is a single `unlockedLevel` integer in localStorage. Scoring uses `calcPushScore` — fewer hits = higher score, floor 200. No retry penalty, no time pressure, no variety in target layout or mechanics beyond material type.

**Step 3 — Question 1 of 3**

What's broken or unsatisfying about the current system? Is the issue the levels themselves (layouts feel samey, too easy/hard), the progression structure (unlock gates feel arbitrary), the scoring (par scores feel disconnected from play), or something else — like wanting a different overall shape to the game?

message.content: Layouts are the same for most of them. Nothing new is really introduced with each level, no new mechanics or interest points.  There's a lack of flow as well, no way to navigate from one level to the next easily

content.text:
**Question 2 of 3**

When you say "new mechanics or interest points" — what direction appeals to you? For example:

- **Environmental hazards** — things in the level that react to or interfere with the rat (bumpers, walls that move, breakable shields in front of targets)
- **Target variety** — targets with different behaviours (armoured targets needing multiple hits, chained targets that shatter together, moving targets)
- **Pivot constraints** — levels where the pivot position is restricted, elevated, or changes mid-round
- **A mix** — some levels introduce one new thing, others layer them

Or is it more about visual/thematic variety — each level *looks and feels* like a distinct place rather than the same arena with different box arrangements?

message.content: New mechanices, the first two especially. Each level also feels very similar, different arrangements or shapes would be good

content.text:
**Question 3 of 3**

On progression specifically — after finishing a level, what should the experience feel like? Currently there's a result screen with Levels / Retry / Next. Is the problem that:

- The **level select** feels disconnected (you don't feel a sense of journey through the levels)
- There's **no incentive to replay** completed levels (once you beat it, no reason to go back)
- The **unlock gate** is too blunt (clear level N to unlock N+1 with no nuance)
- Or something more structural — like wanting a **world map** feel, or **staged acts** with a boss/climax level

lastPrompt: New mechanices, the first two especially. Each level also feels very similar, different arrangements or shapes would be good

message.content: Levels feel disconnected, though maybe we can fix that with styling. Staged acts could also be interesting

content.text:
Good, I have enough to propose approaches.

**Step 4 — Proposed approaches**

I'd recommend **B — Acts + shields + bumpers** — it introduces the most distinct new feel per level while keeping implementation grounded in the existing physics system. Here are the options:

**A — Acts + shape variety only:** Replace the 5 levels with ~9 grouped into 3 acts (Sewer / Warehouse / Lab). New target shapes (circles, angled rects, stacked towers) and varied pivot positions. No new mechanics, just better layout design. Trade-off: immediately noticeable improvement in variety, minimal code change — but still just boxes and circles with no surprises.

**B — Acts + destructible shields + bumpers (recommended):** Same 3-act structure. Act 1 introduces the game with varied shapes. Act 2 introduces **destructible shields** — breakable glass/wood panels placed in front of main targets that the rat must smash through first (each shield has its own HP, destroyed when hit hard enough). Act 3 introduces **bumpers** — fixed circular obstacles that deflect the rat mid-swing, forcing different approach angles. Trade-off: two genuinely new mechanics that change how you think about each swing; requires adding per-obstacle HP and a new bumper body type.

**C — Acts + shields + moving targets:** As above but Act 3 uses oscillating targets instead of bumpers — targets slide back and forth, requiring timing. Trade-off: most mechanically interesting but adds per-frame target movement to the game loop and makes consistent scoring harder to balance.

Which direction?

**Step 5 — Design, Section 1: What's being built**

**9 levels across 3 acts**, each act with a distinct visual theme and a new mechanic introduced mid-game.

**Act 1 — "The Sewer" (levels 1–3):** Tutorial act. Varied target shapes (rectangles, circles, angled blocks), varied pivot heights and string lengths. No new mechanics — teaches combo play and angle reading. Levels escalate in target count and arrangement complexity.

**Act 2 — "The Warehouse" (levels 4–6):** Introduces **destructible shields** — glass or wood panels placed in front of main targets. Shields use the existing `evaluateImpact` logic: hit fast enough and they shatter (SHATTER outcome = removed from world); hit too slowly and the rat barely loses HP and bounces off. Player must build swing speed to break through. Hitting a shield gives minimal rat HP drain; the main target behind it can't be reached until the shield is gone.

**Act 3 — "The Lab" (levels 7–9):** Introduces **bumpers** — static circular obstacles with high restitution that deflect the rat. They never break. Each level arranges them to create routing puzzles — the player must angle the swing to route around or ricochet off bumpers to reach the target.

**Progression:** Level select groups levels into act sections with act names and completion state. Completing the last level of an act shows a brief "ACT CLEAR" screen before the next act unlocks.

Does this section look right before I continue?

**Section 2: How it fits the existing architecture**

- **`levels.js`** — replace 5 levels with 9; add `act` field and `actName` per act; extend target schema with optional `isShield: true` flag; add optional `bumpers[]` array per level; circles via `shape: 'circle'`; angled rects via existing `rectangle` + new `angle` field
- **`physics.js`** — `spawnTargets`: add circle/polygon shape support; tag shield bodies with `plugin.isShield = true`; new `spawnBumpers(bumpers)` returning bumper bodies; bumpers are static circles with `restitution: 0.85`
- **`main.js`** — push-mode collision handler gets a shield branch: if hit body is a shield, run `evaluateImpact` to test break (SHATTER = remove shield, emit particles; SURVIVE = minimal rat HP drain); normal rat HP drain only when hitting non-shield targets; pass bumper bodies to renderer
- **`renderer.js`** — `drawTargets`: handle circle bodies using `body.circleRadius`; shields drawn thinner and brighter to read as "breakable"; new `drawBumpers` function (metallic circles with a shine)
- **`ui.js`** — `buildLevelSelect`: group cards by `act`, render act name as a section header; add "ACT CLEAR" panel to result flow
- **No changes to:** scoring formula, audio, input, test suite, yoyo/rat variants

Does this section look right?

**Section 3: Implementation steps**

1. **Design 9 level configs in `levels.js`** — write all level data first: act assignments, themes (background/ground colours), target shapes and placements, shield positions (act 2+), bumper positions (act 3+), pivot points, string lengths, par scores
2. **`physics.js`** — add circle/angle support to `spawnTargets`; tag shield bodies with `plugin.isShield`; add `spawnBumpers()`; expose `getBumperBodies()` export
3. **`main.js`** — shield collision branch in push-mode handler; call `spawnBumpers` in `startLevel`; pass bumper bodies to renderer
4. **`renderer.js`** — circle target rendering; shield visual treatment (bright, thin-bordered); `drawBumpers` (metallic with highlight ring)
5. **`ui.js`** — act-grouped level select with section headers; "ACT CLEAR" result state
6. **Balance pass** — playtest shield break thresholds and bumper placement; adjust par scores

---

That's the full design. Approve to proceed, or anything to revisit?
Logging the decision and updating the action plan first.

# /brainstorm

Mandatory design gate for new features, components, and non-trivial implementation tasks.
Explores intent, surfaces approaches, and gets design approval before any implementation begins.

## Usage
```
/brainstorm [topic]     # start a brainstorm session for a specific topic
/brainstorm             # start with the current action plan item
```

---

## Hard Gate

Do NOT write code, scaffold files, or take any implementation action until a design has been
presented and the user has given explicit approval. This applies to every project and every
task regardless of apparent simplicity.

---

## Step 1 — Scope check

Assess whether the task warrants a brainstorm session.

**Always brainstorm (never skip unilaterally):**
- New features or user-facing capabilities
- New components, services, or modules
- API or schema changes
- Integrations with external systems
- Refactors that affect how multiple parts of the system interact

**Potentially skippable — ask the user first:**
- Single-file edits with no API, interface, or schema changes
- Bug fixes where the root cause and fix are both unambiguous
- Config or documentation-only changes
- Tasks the user has already described in sufficient implementation detail

If the task falls in the potentially skippable category:
> "This looks like it might be straightforward enough to skip brainstorming — [one-sentence
> reason]. Worth going through the design process, or shall we proceed directly?"

Wait for the user's response. Only skip with explicit confirmation. If in doubt, brainstorm.

---

## Step 2 — Explore context

Read the following before asking any questions:
- `CLAUDE.md` — project overview, constraints, tech stack, guidelines
- `project-state.json` — current activity, action plan, decisions log, open questions (if present)
- Recent commits: `git log --oneline -10` — what has changed recently (if a git repo)

Use this context to avoid asking questions the codebase already answers.

---

## Step 3 — Clarifying questions

Ask one question at a time. Stop when you understand:
- **Purpose** — what problem does this solve, and for whom?
- **Constraints** — technical, time, or scope limits
- **Success criteria** — how will you know it's done?

Target 2–4 questions. Do not ask about things already clear from context.

---

## Step 4 — Propose approaches

Present 2–3 distinct approaches with trade-offs. Lead with a recommendation:

> "I'd recommend **[approach]** — [one-line reason]. Here are the options:
>
> **A — [Name]:** [description]. Trade-off: [pro vs. con].
> **B — [Name]:** [description]. Trade-off: [pro vs. con].
> **C — [Name]:** [description]. Trade-off: [pro vs. con]."

Wait for the user to select or redirect before continuing.

---

## Step 5 — Present design

Present the design in sections, confirming each before moving on. Scale each section to its
complexity — a few sentences for simple changes, more detail for complex ones.

Cover in order:
1. **What's being built** — the feature or component in plain terms
2. **How it fits the existing architecture** — where it lives, what it touches, what it doesn't
3. **Implementation steps** — the first 3–5 concrete tasks

Ask after each section:
> "Does this section look right before I continue?"

---

## Step 6 — Hard gate

Once all sections are presented, request explicit approval:
> "That's the full design. Approve to proceed, or let me know what to revisit."

Do not begin implementation until the user explicitly approves.

---

## Step 7 — Update project state

If a `project-state.json` exists in the project root, after approval:

1. Append a `decisions` log entry:
   ```json
   {
     "date": "<YYYY-MM-DD>",
     "decision": "<one-line description of the chosen approach>",
     "rationale": "<why this approach was chosen over the alternatives>"
   }
   ```

2. Add concrete implementation steps from the approved design as new `pending` entries in
   the action plan. Assign sequential IDs continuing from the current highest. Mark any
   item the design supersedes as `"status": "superseded"` rather than removing it.
   Set the first new task as `current_activity`.

3. Report:
   > "Design approved and logged. Action plan updated with [N] implementation tasks.
   > Ready to build."

# /impl-review

Post-implementation review — checks divergence from the brainstorm plan, updates
documentation on the spot, and signals the commit can proceed. Run before every commit.

## Usage
```
/impl-review        # run after completing an implementation task
```

---

## Step 1 — Read context

Read the following before doing anything else:
- `project-state.json` — most recent brainstorm decisions entry, action plan item statuses (if present)
- `git diff HEAD` — what actually changed in this implementation (if a git repo)
- `CLAUDE.md` and `ARCHITECTURE.md` (if present) — current documented state

If no brainstorm decisions entry exists, note this and proceed with the checklist only.

---

## Step 2 — AI divergence assessment

---

## Step 2 — Check for pre-commit blockers

Scan the staged and unstaged changes for the following. If any are found,
flag them to the user and resolve before committing:

| Check | What to look for |
|---|---|
| Debug code | `console.log`, `debugger`, `TODO`, `FIXME`, `HACK` left in production paths |
| Secrets / env files | `.env`, `.env.local`, `*.key`, `*.pem`, `credentials*`, `secrets*` staged or touched |

| Accidental bulk adds | Ensure `node_modules/`, `*.db`, `*.db-wal`, `*.db-shm` are not staged |

If a blocker is found, stop and report it. Do not proceed until the user
confirms the issue is resolved or intentionally accepted.

---

## Step 3 — Segregate changes into logical commits

Examine the diff for changes that serve **different purposes**. Split into
separate commits when changes fall into clearly different categories. Use
judgment — do not split what belongs together.

- Different in type and unrelated in purpose (e.g. a bug fix + a new feature)
- Touching different subsystems for different reasons
- Mix of functional change and documentation/config update with no coupling

**Keep together when:**
- A feature spans multiple files but is one cohesive unit of work
- A fix requires touching both the implementation and its test/config

For each logical group, stage only those files, then proceed through
Steps 4–5 before moving to the next group.

Each of the 6 substeps below requires a suggestion followed by explicit user
approval before proceeding. Present the suggestion clearly, then **pause and
wait**. Do not advance to the next substep until the user confirms or amends.

rationale. Ask the user to confirm or change it.

| Type | Use for |
|---|---|

| `fix` | Bug fix |
| `refactor` | Code change that neither fixes a bug nor adds a feature |
| `chore` | Tooling, dependencies, config, build changes |
| `docs` | Documentation only |
| `style` | Formatting, whitespace — no logic change |

- Imperative mood: "add", "fix", "remove" — not "added", "fixes", "removes"

it has. Do not just restate the subject line. Rules:
- One blank line between subject and body
- Wrap at ~72 characters per line

> "Suggested body:
> [draft body text]
> Approve, or would you like any changes?"

**Wait for approval.**

or public interfaces.

A browser-based physics game. Swing a rat on a string into targets to smash them. Chain hits to build a combo multiplier and beat the par score.

ES6 modules require HTTP — you can't open `index.html` directly via `file://`. Serve the project root with any static file server:

```bash
python3 -m http.server 8080

npx serve .

# Caddy, nginx, or any other static server also works
```

- **Move the mouse** to swing the rat. The pivot follows your cursor.
- **Chain hits** within one second to build a combo multiplier (up to 3×).

- **Fewer hits = higher score.** A one-hit smash scores 3000; each extra hit costs 500.

| 3 — The Lab | Clinical | **Bumpers** — deflect the rat around obstacles |

```bash
npx vitest run        # single pass
npx vitest            # watch mode
```

Vanilla JS · ES6 modules · Canvas 2D · [Matter.js 0.19.0](https://brm.io/matter-js/) · Web Audio API · [Vitest](https://vitest.dev/)
